## Using Census Records to Trace Your Family

The FamilySearch wiki provided guidance from two key pages — **United States Census — Background** and **United States Census — Strategy** — covering:

### What Census Records Contain
Census records vary by decade. Earlier censuses (pre-1850) list only the head of household by name, with other members counted by age/sex brackets. From **1850 onward**, every person in the household is listed by name, along with age, birthplace, occupation, and other details. Later censuses (1880+) add relationship to head of household, parents' birthplaces, and more.

### How to Search on FamilySearch
- Go to [FamilySearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) and use the **Search > Records** feature

- Try name variants and wildcards if an exact search turns up nothing

### Strategy for Tracing a Family
- **Work backwards** — start with what you know and move to earlier censuses
- **Follow the family** across multiple census years to track migration, births, deaths, and household changes
- **Cross-reference** with other record types (vital records, land, probate) to fill gaps
- Use the **household context** — neighbors and nearby families were often relatives or came from the same area of origin

# FamilySearch Wiki: Census Records to Trace Family

United States federal census records are among the most important genealogical sources. A census was taken every ten years beginning in 1790. FamilySearch has a census collection with an index and images for each federal census year from 1790 through 1950. Most of these censuses are also on subscription sites such as Ancestry, Findmypast, and MyHeritage, which require a paid subscription for full access. To search census records, go to FamilySearch.org, click Search, then Records, enter your ancestor's name, and filter by record type 'Census, Voter Lists.'

What a census recorded about each household member changed over time. From 1790 through 1840, only the head of household is named, and everyone else is counted only as tally marks within age and sex categories. From 1850 through 1870, every free person in the household is listed by name with age, sex, and birthplace, but relationship to the head of household is not stated. Beginning in 1880, every person is listed by name together with their relationship to the head of household.

By tracing a family through multiple census years, you can watch children grow up, track a family's migration, and identify previously unknown relatives. Each census decade can point you to a new location or a maiden name. When searching, try alternate spellings of surnames and consider that ages reported in different census years may vary by several years.

## Sources

- [United States Census — Background](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Census#Background)
- [United States Census — Strategy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/United_States_Census#Strategy)

args.notes:
# FamilySearch Wiki: Irish church records

Church records are among the most important sources for Irish genealogy research. The two main denominations that kept parish registers in Ireland were the Roman Catholic Church and the Church of Ireland (Anglican). Roman Catholic registers generally begin in the early 1800s, while Church of Ireland registers often start earlier, in the 1700s. Many original registers were destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office fire, but microfilmed copies and transcriptions survive. FamilySearch has digitized and indexed a large collection of Irish Catholic and Church of Ireland parish registers, which are freely searchable at FamilySearch.org.

To find Irish church records on FamilySearch, go to FamilySearch.org and click Search, then Records. Enter your ancestor's name and select Ireland as the country. Filter results by record type to narrow to church records including baptisms, marriages, and burials. The National Library of Ireland also holds a large collection of Catholic parish registers on microfilm, many of which have been digitized and are available online. The Representative Church Body Library in Dublin holds Church of Ireland registers not destroyed in 1922.

Irish church records typically contain baptism (christening) records listing the child's name, baptism date, parents' names, and sometimes the townland or parish of residence. Marriage records list the names of the bride and groom, the date and place of marriage, and witnesses. Burial records list the name of the deceased and the burial date. Earlier records may contain less detail. Some registers also include sponsor names for baptisms, which can help identify other family members.

## Sources

- [Ireland Church Records — Overview of Irish Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records#Overview_of_Irish_Church_Records)
- [Ireland Church Records — Finding Church Records on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records#Finding_Church_Records_on_FamilySearch)
- [Ireland Church Records — What Church Records Contain](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records#What_Church_Records_Contain)

Here's what the FamilySearch Wiki research uncovered on finding Italian birth records:

---

## How to Find Italian Birth Records

Two main types of records cover births in Italy:

### 1. Civil Registration Records
Italy's civil registration (stato civile) began in different regions at different times:
- **Kingdom of Italy (most of the north and center):** civil registration started **1866**
- **Kingdom of Naples / Two Sicilies (south):** Napoleon introduced civil registration as early as **1809**, making southern Italy one of the earliest areas covered
- **Tuscany and the Papal States:** varied start dates, generally mid-19th century

Civil birth records (atti di nascita) typically include the child's name, date and place of birth, parents' names, and witnesses.

### 2. Church (Parish) Records
Before civil registration, Catholic parish registers (registri parrocchiali) recorded baptisms. These can go back to the 1500s–1600s in many areas. They contain baptism date, child's name, parents' names, and godparents.

---

### How to Access These Records

- **FamilySearch.org** has digitized millions of Italian civil and church records, searchable by town (comune). Start with the [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/catalog) and search by place name.
- Records are organized by **comune** (municipality), so knowing the specific town of origin is essential.
- Many records are available as **free browsable images** on FamilySearch, even if not fully indexed.

---

**Next step:** Search the FamilySearch Catalog for the specific *comune* where your ancestor was born to find available collections of civil or parish birth records.

# FamilySearch Wiki: Italian Birth Records

Civil registration (Stato Civile) of births, marriages, and deaths began in most of Italy in 1809 under Napoleonic rule, lapsed in many regions after 1815, and resumed nationwide in 1866 following unification. Civil birth records (atti di nascita) are the single most useful source for Italian genealogy after 1866. They record the child's name, the date and place of birth, and the names, ages, occupations, and residence of both parents.

Before civil registration, and as a parallel source afterward, Catholic parish registers (registri parrocchiali) recorded baptisms. German church records are among the most valuable genealogical sources for tracing German ancestors. Here is the guidance from the FamilySearch Research Wiki:

   - **State archives (Landesarchive)** — original registers are often held at regional German archives.

# FamilySearch Wiki: German Church Records

Church records (Kirchenbücher) are the most important source for German genealogy before civil registration. Protestant (Evangelisch) and Catholic (Katholisch) parishes recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials, with many registers beginning in the 1600s and some Catholic registers reaching back to the mid-1500s. Each register is kept by the parish, not by the town, so identifying the correct parish is the essential first step.

To find the parish that served an ancestor's village, use a gazetteer. Meyers Orts- und Verkehrs-Lexikon des Deutschen Reichs lists every place in the 1871-1918 German Empire and identifies the civil registration office and the Protestant and Catholic parishes serving it.

Many German church records have been microfilmed or digitized and are listed in the FamilySearch Catalog under the parish or town name. Others remain only at the parish, the regional church archive (Landeskirchliches Archiv or Kirchenbuchamt), or on subscription sites such as Archion (Protestant) and Matricula (Catholic).

Church records (Kirchenbücher) are the most important source for German genealogy before civil registration. Protestant (Evangelisch) and Catholic (Katholisch) parishes recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials, with many registers beginning in the 1600s and some Catholic registers reaching back to the mid-1500s. Many German church records have been microfilmed or digitized and are listed in the FamilySearch Catalog under the parish or town name. Others remain only at the parish, the regional church archive (Landeskirchliches Archiv or Kirchenbuchamt), or on subscription sites such as Archion (Protestant) and Matricula (Catholic).

# FamilySearch Wiki: Immigration Records

Immigration records document the arrival of individuals into a country and are a key source for tracing ancestors who moved from one country to another. For the United States, passenger arrival records (also called ship manifests or passenger lists) are the primary immigration records. These records were created at the port of arrival and typically list the passenger's name, age, occupation, country of origin, and destination. To find immigration records on FamilySearch, go to FamilySearch.org, click Search, then Records, and enter your ancestor's name. You can filter by record type and country of origin to narrow results. Naturalization records are also useful — they document the process by which an immigrant became a citizen and may include the immigrant's country of birth, arrival date, and port of entry. Naturalization records were kept at the local court level and FamilySearch has indexed many of them.

# FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Land Records

Pennsylvania land records are among the oldest in the United States. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds the original land warrant books and patent books dating to the 1680s. Some county deed indexes are available as browse-only images. The Pennsylvania State Archives Warrant Tract Maps are also useful for locating land within the original county boundaries, which changed frequently during the colonial and early statehood periods.

# FamilySearch Wiki: Marriage Records

In the United States, marriage records were typically kept by county clerks, churches, or state vital records offices, depending on the time period and location. Both may include the names of the bride and groom, the date and place of marriage, the names of witnesses, and sometimes the ages and birthplaces of the couple. In some jurisdictions, marriage bonds or banns were also recorded.

Here's what the FamilySearch Wiki research agent found on locating probate and will records for a deceased ancestor:

---

## Finding Probate and Will Records on FamilySearch

**What are probate records?**
Probate records are court documents created when a deceased person's estate was settled. They can include:
- **Wills** – the deceased's instructions for distributing their property
- **Inventories** – lists of the estate's property and its value
- **Administration records** – created when someone died without a will (intestate)
- **Guardian records** – for minor heirs
- **Distribution records** – how assets were divided among heirs

These records are invaluable for genealogy because they often name family members, neighbors, and relationships explicitly.

---

**How to find them on FamilySearch:**

1. **Search the FamilySearch Catalog** – Go to [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/catalog/search) and search by **place** (state and county), then browse under the subject category **"Probate records."** This will show what collections are available and whether they are digitized, microfilmed, or only available at a repository.

2. **Search FamilySearch Records** – Some probate collections have been indexed and can be searched by name at [FamilySearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org/search/). Use the **Keyword** or **Record Type** filter if available.

3. **Check the county courthouse** – Probate records were typically kept by the county court (probate court, surrogate court, or orphans' court depending on the state). If not digitized, you may need to contact the court directly or visit in person.

4. **Look for compiled indexes** – Many states have published statewide or county-level indexes to wills and estates, sometimes available through libraries or genealogical societies.

---

The guidance and the source wiki pages have been saved to your project's research log for future reference. When you're ready, you can start your search in the **FamilySearch Catalog** by filtering to your ancestor's specific state and county under "Probate records."
